passage.title: How Plastic Reaches the River
passage.audio: A science lesson last week followed a plastic bottle from a street bin to the river. The teacher showed a short film in which wind blew light bottles out of an open bin and rain then carried them along the gutter. passage.title: An Experiment with Melting Ice
passage.audio: In the laboratory we tested how ice melts in different places. Each pair received three pieces of ice of the same size. We put one in the sun on the window, one in the shade, and one in a cup of warm water. We checked them every two minutes and wrote down the time when each piece disappeared. The ice in warm water melted first, and the ice in the shade lasted the longest. One pair made a mistake because they used a smaller piece in the sun, so their times could not be compared fairly. The class discussed why a fair test needs the same starting size. We will repeat the experiment next week with salt on one piece.

passage.title: The Story of a Local Bridge
passage.audio: The old stone bridge in our town is more than one hundred years old. It was built so that farmers could take vegetables to the market on the other side of the river. During a flood in nineteen ninety-eight the water rose almost to the top, but the bridge did not fall. Last year engineers found cracks in two stones and closed the bridge for a month while they were repaired. Now there is a weight limit, and heavy trucks must use the new road to the south. Many people still walk across in the evening because the view of the river is beautiful. A small board at the entrance tells this history in a few lines.

passage.title: City Trees and Summer Shade
passage.audio: A city report on summer heat said that streets with many trees were several degrees cooler in the afternoon than streets with almost no trees. The trees also help rainwater sink into the ground instead of rushing into the drains. The report asked the city to plant more trees along the hottest roads, not only in parks that already look green in photos. The writer of the report said shade is not a luxury. It is a way to keep the city safer in hot years.

passage.audio: The night before a test, some students stay up very late to read every page again. Research discussed in our health class suggests that this plan often fails. passage.title: Why a Small Sample Can Mislead

passage.title: Why Cramming Fails Overnight
passage.audio: The night before a history paper, some students try to read the whole book in one sitting. A psychology talk at school explained why this cramming often feels hard and still fails. The brain can hold only a limited amount of new material in a short time, and fatigue makes even that amount weaker by morning. Several students have now made a calendar that places a little history practice on four evenings, not one.

passage.audio: Group projects can teach cooperation, but they can also grow until a few students carry most of the work. passage.title: When Two Facts Rise Together
passage.audio: A science club looked at a graph that showed ice cream sales and swimming accidents rising in the same months. Someone in the room joked that ice cream must cause the accidents. The club then listed other facts that also rise in those months, such as hot weather and more people at the beach. The teacher used the example to explain a basic rule: when two numbers rise together, one does not automatically cause the other. There may be a third factor, or the pattern may be a chance result in a short set of months. The club later found a second graph in which sales and accidents did not move together after the weather was taken into account. Members now write a question beside every striking graph: what else could explain this pattern. The habit does not make graphs useless. It makes them harder to misuse in a headline or in a casual joke.

passage.audio: A social studies project followed a package from an online order to a door in our city. They also wrote that a fair system would show how pay is calculated and would offer a way to speak to a person when an account is frozen. passage.title: A Heatwave on Two Streets
passage.audio: During a heatwave last August, a health team compared two streets that were only three blocks apart. One street had old trees, light coloured walls and many people at home in the afternoon. The other had almost no shade, dark roofs and more elderly residents who lived alone. Temperatures on the second street were higher, and more people there needed medical help for heat illness. The team said the difference was not only the weather, which was the same over the whole district. It was the design of the street and the support around people who cannot leave their rooms easily. The city will now plant trees on the hotter street first, and a volunteer group will telephone older residents on the first morning of a heat warning. The study is a reminder that the same heat can be a different danger depending on where you live and who can check on you.

passage.title: Repeating a Famous Result
passage.audio: A psychology paper that was widely taught for years could not be repeated by three later teams. The original study had a small sample and reported a large effect. When the later teams used a larger sample and wrote their plan before they saw the results, the effect became small or disappeared. The finding does not prove that the first team was dishonest. It shows why one published result is a beginning, not a final verdict. Our science teacher asked us to look for a sentence about sample size and about whether a study has been repeated, before we treat a headline as settled. She also said a failed repeat is information, not an insult. The class now keeps a short checklist on the lab wall: size, plan, and repeat. The list will not make every paper perfect, but it will make us slower to be sure.

passage.title: Who Is Missing from a Survey
passage.audio: A student survey on after school jobs was sent by email to everyone in the grade. About one third of the students replied, and most of those who replied had a regular internet connection at home and time in the evening to write. The results said that most students found jobs easy to manage with homework. Then a teacher noticed that almost no replies had come from students who work late in family shops, and that some of those students have little time for email. When a second, shorter survey was given on paper during class, the picture changed: more students reported tiredness and less time for homework. The class learned that a survey can miss the very people whose experience would change the conclusion. From now on they will ask, for every survey, who was invited, who could reply easily, and who is absent from the results. A question that is not asked of everyone can still be useful, but it should not speak for the whole grade.

passage.title: When an App Chooses for You
passage.audio: A music app that many students use does not only play songs they select. It also builds a list based on what they have already played and on what people like them have played. Over a month, two classmates compared their lists and found that the songs were becoming more similar to their past choices and less surprising. One of them then spent a week choosing only from a library list in the school music room, and her app list slowly became wider again. The class used the story to talk about how a convenient tool can narrow taste without a clear warning. The point was not to abandon the app. It was to notice when a machine is choosing, to try a source outside the usual list, and to ask what the company gains when a user stays inside a familiar set of songs. A free list can still have a hidden cost if it quietly reduces what you hear.

passage.title: A Quiet Room for Exams
passage.audio: During final exams, a student with attention difficulties asked for a quiet room. The school at first said that all students must sit in the main hall so that the test is the same for everyone. A counsellor then explained that the hall is not the same experience for every student: noise that is a small distraction for one person can make another person lose a whole section of the paper. After a meeting, the school agreed that a quiet room is a change in the setting, not a change in the questions or the time, and that it can make the test fairer rather than easier. Two other students were also offered the room after they described similar problems. The exam board later wrote that equal treatment does not always mean the same room, but it does mean the same chance to show what you know. The quiet room will now be booked in advance for every official exam week.

passage.title: Carbon Labels on Everyday Food
passage.audio: A supermarket in our city has begun to print a small carbon label on some everyday foods, such as milk, rice and apples. The number is meant to show the greenhouse gas linked to producing and transporting that item, so that shoppers can compare two similar products. A class visit found that the labels helped when two milks were side by side, but they were less useful when a product had no label at all, or when the number was printed in a colour that was hard to read. A manager said the store will add labels to more items this year and will use a darker print. The students also noted a risk: a label can become a substitute for thinking about waste, if people buy a slightly lower number and then throw food away at home. Their report says labels are a tool, not a complete answer, and that a fair label should be clear, complete and hard to ignore. The store has asked the class to test the new print in March.
